newsitem.title: CHINA: HK court ruling dents autonomy, say experts.
newsitem.headline: HK court ruling dents autonomy, say experts.

text.p: A landmark court ruling confirming the legality of a China-appointed legislature has undermined Hong Kong's autonomy after its return to Chinese rule, legal experts said on Wednesday.
But Hong Kong's stock market gave the territory a big vote of confidence by powering to a new record high on Wednesday -- one month after Britain handed the colony back to China.
The Hang Seng index breached 16,000 points to prove that political polemics now have little effect on business in this bustling bastion of capitalism.
Nevertheless fresh legal challenges lie ahead for the Provisional Legislative Council (PLC), which has been making laws since China resumed sovereignty.
An appeals court quashed a challenge to the PLC on Tuesday and ruled it was legitimately created by China's parliament, the National People's Congress (NPC).
A panel of three judges said Hong Kong courts had no power to rule on the legality of the PLC because it was appointed by the NPC.
The historic ruling in the case, which sprung from a criminal conspiracy trial, has rescued the post-colonial government from a potential constitutional crisis -- for the time being at least.
Defence lawyers in the criminal case argued that British Common Law lapsed with the handover and that the new legislature had failed to adopt pre-handover laws, creating a legal vacuum.
Hong Kong Human Rights Monitor watchdog group decried Tuesday's ruling as a "sad day for Hong Kong".
"The decision undermines the rule of law, by putting certain Chinese bodies above the law and removes any basis for the autonomy of Hong Kong," it said in a statement.

Law professor Peter Wesley-Smith of Hong Kong University said the rule of law and the duty of courts to uphold Hong Kong's constitution, the Basic Law, which promises a high degree of autonomy after July 1, stood in jeopardy.

"They've abandoned legal arguments. They've said there is a sovereign entity in the new system, the NPC, and the courts are helpless in front of it," Smith said. "I don't think that shows respect for the rule of law or the promises made."
But provisional legislator Selina Chow, who is also a member of the pro-business Liberal Party, welcomed the ruling as necessary for Hong Kong "to get on with life", and for the PLC.

"The judgment has a positive effect for our future because without it, the dispute can go on and on as it has for the last few months, which is not doing Hong Kong any good," she said. "We should get settled and forget about all these disputes."

But Chow and her colleagues may be disappointed. A team of lawyers are gearing up for a court battle against a new immigration law that threatens to deport child illegal immigrants back to mainland China, although they had legal right of abode here after July 1 under the Basic Law, Hong Kong's mini-constitution.
Some 125 children and their families have won government legal aid to fight their cases. The new law was enacted by the PLC just days after it was installed.
The lawyers, who will choose a few representative cases, will appear before a Hong Kong judge on August 4, who will decide when the hearing will begin, a government spokesman said.
Local newspapers indicated the latest victory by the new government and the PLC might be shortlived.

A cartoon in the English-language South China Morning Post depicted PLC speaker Rita Fan celebrating with champagne on a balcony and looking askance as a fellow legislator whispers to her, "one down, more to come?"
